title: Multiclass Classification on the Iris Dataset
text:
This project develops a case study in multiclass classification using the classic Iris flower dataset.
Rather than focusing solely on predictive performance, the project emphasizes the full classification workflow: exploratory data analysis, feature engineering, and rigorous comparison of multiple models through cross-validation.
The final objective is to identify which measurements best separate the three Iris species and which model classifies them most reliably.

title: Multiclass Classification on the Iris Dataset
text:
Problem Statement
Given sepal and petal measurements for an Iris flower, the system must:

Explore and understand the dataset.
Engineer and evaluate additional predictive features.
Train and compare multiple classification models.
Predict the species for unseen observations.

title: Multiclass Classification on the Iris Dataset
text:
Methodology
The project follows a structured machine learning pipeline:

Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)
Feature engineering (derived measurements, dimensionality reduction for visualization)
Feature scaling
Baseline and comparison models
Logistic Regression
K-Nearest Neighbors
Decision Tree
Random Forest
Support Vector Machine
Cross-validation and model comparison
Final model selection and evaluation

title: Multiclass Classification on the Iris Dataset
text:
Dataset
The project uses the Iris Flower Dataset from Kaggle.
The dataset contains sepal and petal measurements for 150 Iris flowers, evenly split across three species:

Sepal length and width (cm)
Petal length and width (cm)
Species: Iris-setosa, Iris-versicolor, Iris-virginica

The objective is to predict species from the four measurements.

title: Modeling and Evaluation
text:
Comparison of classification models on the engineered Iris features, using cross-validation given how small the dataset is.
Code
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate, cross_val_predict
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay

sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")
RANDOM_STATE = 42

title: Modeling and Evaluation
text:
Model comparison via cross-validation
With only 150 rows, a single train/test split gives a noisy estimate. Stratified 5-fold cross-validation is used instead so each model’s score reflects the full dataset.


Code
models = {
    "Logistic Regression": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "KNN": KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5),
    "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
    "SVM (RBF)": SVC(kernel="rbf", random_state=RANDOM_STATE),
}

cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=RANDOM_STATE)




Code
results = []
for name, model in models.items():
    scores = cross_validate(model, X, y, cv=cv, scoring=["accuracy", "f1_macro"])
    results.append({
        "model": name,
        "accuracy_mean": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        "accuracy_std": scores["test_accuracy"].std(),
        "f1_macro_mean": scores["test_f1_macro"].mean(),
        "f1_macro_std": scores["test_f1_macro"].std(),
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results).sort_values("f1_macro_mean", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

title: Modeling and Evaluation

Confusion matrices
Out-of-fold predictions from cross-validation, one confusion matrix per model.


Code
labels = sorted(y.unique())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(models), figsize=(4 * len(models), 4))
for ax, (name, model) in zip(axes, models.items()):
    y_pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=cv)
    cm = confusion_matrix(y, y_pred, labels=labels)
    ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=labels).plot(ax=ax, colorbar=False, xticks_rotation=45)
    ax.set_title(name)
fig.tight_layout()

title: Modeling and Evaluation
text:
Decision boundaries on the 2D projection
For visualization only, each model is refit on the PCA 2D coordinates from notebook 01 (not the full feature set used above) so its decision regions can be plotted.


Code
def plot_decision_boundary(ax, model, X2, y2, title):
    x_min, x_max = X2[:, 0].min() - 1, X2[:, 0].max() + 1
    y_min, y_max = X2[:, 1].min() - 1, X2[:, 1].max() + 1
    xx, yy = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(x_min, x_max, 300), np.linspace(y_min, y_max, 300))

    model.fit(X2, y2)
    codes = y2.astype("category")
    preds = model.predict(np.c_[xx.ravel(), yy.ravel()])
    preds = pd.Series(preds, dtype=codes.dtype).cat.codes.values.reshape(xx.shape)

    ax.contourf(xx, yy, preds, alpha=0.3, cmap="Set2")
    ax.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], c=codes.cat.codes, cmap="Set2", edgecolor="k", s=20)
    ax.set_title(title)




Code
X2 = data[["pca_1", "pca_2"]].values
y2 = data["species"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(models), figsize=(4 * len(models), 4))
for ax, (name, model) in zip(axes, models.items()):
    plot_decision_boundary(ax, model, X2, y2, name)
fig.tight_layout()

Feature importance
Tree-based models expose feature importances directly, fit here on the full feature set (not just the 2D projection).

title: Modeling and Evaluation
text:
Summary
Cross-validated macro F1 ranks the five models within a narrow band, with KNN and SVM (RBF) tying for best (0.967), Decision Tree close behind (0.966), Logistic Regression at 0.960, and Random Forest lowest at 0.953. Given the tie, KNN is selected as the best model.
Across every model, all 5 misclassifications (out of 150) fall on the versicolor/virginica boundary (3 versicolor predicted as virginica, 2 virginica predicted as versicolor); setosa is classified perfectly in every fold. This matches the separability story from notebook 01: setosa is linearly separable from the other two species, while versicolor and virginica overlap enough on petal measurements to be the main source of error for any model.

title: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) and feature engineering
text:
Separability story
Setosa is linearly separable from the other two species on nearly every feature, especially petal length and petal width. Versicolor and virginica overlap more, with petal measurements offering the clearest (though imperfect) separation. This overlap is the main source of classification error to watch for in the modeling notebook.

title: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) and feature engineering
text:
Feature engineering
The raw features are already clean, so engineering focuses on derived measurements that add analytical value: areas and length/width ratios between petals and sepals.

data["sepal_area"] = data["sepal_length"] * data["sepal_width"]
data["petal_area"] = data["petal_length"] * data["petal_width"]
data["petal_sepal_length_ratio"] = data["petal_length"] / data["sepal_length"]
data["petal_sepal_width_ratio"] = data["petal_width"] / data["sepal_width"]

Scaling
Standardize features for the distance-based models used in the modeling notebook (KNN, SVM).


Code
feature_cols = [
    "sepal_length",
    "sepal_width",
    "petal_length",
    "petal_width",
    "sepal_area",
    "petal_area",
    "petal_sepal_length_ratio",
    "petal_sepal_width_ratio",
]

scaler = StandardScaler()
scaled = scaler.fit_transform(data[feature_cols])
scaled = pd.DataFrame(scaled, columns=feature_cols, index=data.index)

title: Exploratory data analysis (EDA) and feature engineering
text:
2D projection (PCA and LDA)
Used later to visualize decision boundaries on a 2D plane.


Code
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pca_coords = pca.fit_transform(scaled)
data["pca_1"] = pca_coords[:, 0]
data["pca_2"] = pca_coords[:, 1]

lda = LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(n_components=2)
lda_coords = lda.fit_transform(scaled, data["species"])
data["lda_1"] = lda_coords[:, 0]
data["lda_2"] = lda_coords[:, 1]

print("PCA explained variance ratio:", pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
